opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to two things: the problem and the people.

I'd spent years in academia working on language models and agents, going back to the early GPT work and then research on how to get these systems to actually act in the world and complete tasks, not just generate text. What always stayed with me was the gap between what these models can do in a demo and what it takes for them to work reliably when something real is at stake. So when I started talking with Bret and Clay, what struck me was that they saw customer-facing agents as the place where that gap had to be closed. When an agent talks to someone on behalf of a company, it has to be accurate, follow policy, take the right actions in real systems, and represent the brand well, all in a messy, open-ended conversation. From a research perspective, that's an incredibly rich problem, and it's one you can't fully appreciate from the outside.

The second part was the conviction that this wasn't a research side project attached to a business. They genuinely believed that research and product needed to be tightly connected, and that getting agents to work well in production would raise new scientific questions. How do you evaluate an agent in a meaningful way? How do you simulate realistic users? How do you make these systems improve over time? And there's something really valuable about having real-world feedback, because in academia you often have to guess at what matters, whereas here you see very quickly where things break.

And then, of course, there was the timing. It felt like the technology had just crossed the threshold where this was possible, but the hard work of making it dependable was still ahead of us. When you have a rare moment like that, along with a team that has built great companies before and really cares about doing this right, it's hard to pass up. So for me, it felt like a chance to take ideas I'd been thinking about for a long time and see them have an impact at real scale.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I'd spent most of my career on the research side, and for a long time I was honestly skeptical about leaving that. At Princeton my group was working on language agents, things like SWE-bench and ReAct and WebShop, and the question we kept circling was: what happens when these models actually have to do things in the world, not just answer questions in a benchmark? And that's a question you can only partially answer in a lab. At some point you need real users, real stakes, real messiness.

So when I started talking to Bret and Clay, a couple of things clicked. The first was that they weren't treating agents as a feature bolted onto a chatbot. They were treating the agent as the product, and they were obsessed with the unglamorous parts: reliability, evaluation, what happens when the model is wrong in front of a customer. That's exactly the research problem I cared about, just with much higher consequences.

The second was the people. Bret has built products at a scale that very few people have, and Clay deeply understands enterprise. And they were genuinely excited about research, not as a marketing line, but as something that would change what the company could ship. That combination is rare. Usually you get a research culture or a shipping culture, and they're in tension.

And then honestly, the third thing was timing. I'd worked on GPT-1 when the idea that pretraining could generalize was still kind of a bet. I felt a similar inflection with agents. The models were suddenly good enough that the bottleneck moved from capability to everything around capability: tooling, verification, the interface between the model and a real business process. I wanted to be in the place where that bottleneck was most visible. For customer-facing agents, Sierra felt like that place.

So the conviction wasn't that I had all the answers. It was that this was the room where the right questions were being asked, with the resources and the urgency to actually answer them.

astra-6.text: For me, it was the opportunity to bring research and real-world impact closer together. With language models, there’s a big difference between showing that a capability exists and making it useful and reliable for someone. That gap is intellectually exciting to me. Sierra represented an opportunity to work on that—to take the ideas behind these models and help turn them into something people can actually use.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was the opportunity to bring research into a setting where it could be useful to people. With language models, generating a good response is one piece of the puzzle. Building a system that can understand what someone needs, take action, and reliably help them accomplish something is a much broader challenge. That combination of interesting research questions and a concrete purpose was really compelling to me.
